strengths: The core idea of constraining error compensation to orthogonal transformations (formulated as an Orthogonal Procrustes problem) is mathematically clean, geometrically well-motivated, and avoids the severe overfitting/scaling distortions inherent in unconstrained least-squares updates under small calibration sets.
Unlike Ridge regression, RCPU admits a simple closed-form SVD solution without requiring sensitive and expensive hyperparameter tuning for regularization strength.

The paper provides an insightful degrees-of-freedom and geometric stability analysis comparing RCPU with regularized least-squares, explaining why in-sample calibration perplexity does not necessarily translate to downstream benchmark performance.

The experimental evaluation is extensive across perplexity and multiple standard zero-shot reasoning benchmarks (BoolQ, PIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC, OBQA), showing consistent improvements over Wanda-sp, FLAP, and SliceGPT across multiple model sizes (LLaMA-7B, LLaMA-2-13B, Vicuna-7B).
weaknesses: The evaluated model families are somewhat outdated (LLaMA-1, LLaMA-2, Vicuna); testing on modern standard architectures such as LLaMA-3, Mistral, or Qwen 2.5 would significantly strengthen the empirical relevance of the work.

The maximum pruning ratio tested is 30%. In structured pruning literature, higher sparsity regimes (e.g., 40%–50%) often expose the breakdown point and stability boundaries of compensation techniques.

While the paper reports pruning time per layer, it lacks end-to-end wall-clock latency or memory throughput benchmarks of the pruned models during actual inference on real hardware to confirm practical speedups.

The method bundles two distinct components—a new variance-aware column scoring metric and the rotation-constrained compensation. While Figure 3 explores some combinations, a more systematic ablation separating the isolated contribution of the variance-aware score versus WANDA-sp across all downstream benchmarks would improve clarity.

strengths: Clear geometric motivation: using an Orthogonal Procrustes formulation to re-align output representations under a rotation constraint intuitively avoids the scaling and shearing distortions that unconstrained least-squares updates suffer from under limited calibration data.

Hyperparameter-free closed-form solution: unlike Ridge regression which requires an expensive search over the regularization parameter $\lambda$, the Procrustes problem has an analytical solution via SVD that incurs negligible overhead per layer.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the paper provides thorough comparisons across multiple models (Llama-7B, Llama-2-13B, Vicuna-7B), evaluating both perplexity and zero-shot accuracy across seven diverse benchmark datasets.
weaknesses: Inconsistent empirical gains over baselines: On several benchmark settings, RCPU does not consistently outperform existing uncompensated or simpler methods. For example, in Table 7 (Llama-2-13B with $N_{\text{calib}}=128$), plain WANDA-sp achieves higher mean zero-shot accuracy than RCPU at both 10% (67.74 vs. 67.22) and 20% (64.42 vs. 64.09) pruning ratios. On other configurations, margins over FLAP or WANDA-sp are often modest (within 0.2–0.5%).

Conflation of contributions: The paper combines two distinct components—a variance-aware pruning score and rotation-constrained parameter updates. While Figure 3 shows some PPL breakdown, the downstream benchmark evaluations (Tables 2, 3, 6, 7) do not adequately disentangle how much accuracy gain is attributable to the new scoring heuristic versus the orthogonal Procrustes update.

Evaluation restricted to low pruning ratios: Experiments only evaluate conservative pruning ratios up to 30%. In structured pruning literature, evaluating higher ratios (e.g., 40%–50%) is important to understand when and how severely compensation methods break down.

Lack of wall-clock inference speedups: While the paper details memory footprint and parameter counts, it does not benchmark actual latency improvements / wall-clock inference speedups on real hardware to confirm practical acceleration.

strengths: Clear motivation: Restricting parameter updates to orthogonal transformations (Orthogonal Procrustes) directly addresses the overfitting and geometric distortion issues associated with unconstrained least-squares regression under sparse calibration data.

Hyperparameter-free formulation: Unlike ridge regression which requires careful, computationally heavy tuning of the regularization coefficient lambda, the orthogonal Procrustes update admits an exact closed-form solution via SVD.
Intuitive integration: The method operates layerwise without architectural modifications or gradient-based retraining, making it easy to plug into existing one-shot pruning pipelines.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: The core methodological contribution boils down to applying the standard Orthogonal Procrustes problem (solved via SVD) to compensate for column pruning errors, combined with a simple heuristic modification to the Wanda-sp score (multiplying by activation variance). Both components represent relatively incremental additions to existing post-pruning literature.

Marginal empirical gains: Across benchmark evaluation datasets (Tables 2, 3, 6, 7), the performance improvements over the primary baseline (FLAP) are minimal—often within 0.1–0.3% in mean zero-shot accuracy, and FLAP or Wanda-sp even outperforms RCPU on several individual tasks.

Outdated and narrow model evaluation: Experiments are conducted exclusively on older generation models (LLaMA-1 7B, LLaMA-2 13B, and Vicuna-7B) at relatively conservative pruning ratios (up to 30%). Evaluation on contemporary open-source models (such as LLaMA-3/3.1, Mistral, or Qwen2.5) is missing.

Absence of real inference speedup measurements: A primary motivation for structured pruning over unstructured pruning is achieving actual hardware acceleration during inference. The paper reports parameter counts, memory footprints, and pruning times, but omits wall-clock inference latency or throughput comparisons.

strengths: The core idea of constraining post-pruning error compensation to an orthogonal transformation (Orthogonal Procrustes problem) is well-motivated, elegant, and admits an exact, closed-form SVD solution.
Restricting updates to rotations effectively prevents the overfitting, scaling drift, and geometric shear that often degrade unconstrained least-squares updates under limited calibration data.
The paper is clearly written, mathematically sound in its formulation, and provides sensible ablations comparing unconstrained least-squares, rotation, and rotation with isotropic scaling.
weaknesses: Empirical evaluation is overly narrow: experiments are conducted exclusively on a single model (LLaMA-7B). Modern LLM compression benchmarks typically require validation across multiple model families and scales (e.g., LLaMA-2/3, Mistral, Qwen).

Missing crucial baseline: While SliceGPT (Ashkboos et al., 2024) is discussed in the related work as using orthogonal transformations for structured LLM compression, it is omitted from empirical comparison.

Conflation of contributions in main results: RCPU introduces both a variance-aware scoring function and rotation-based compensation. In Table 1 and Table 2, the relative isolated contributions of the variance scoring versus the Procrustes rotation are not fully disentangled against FLAP.

Marginal performance gains over FLAP at higher pruning ratios: At 30% pruning (Table 2), plain RCPU (55.50%) underperforms FLAP (56.20%), while RCPU (Rot.+Scale) achieves 56.34%, representing an incremental gain of only +0.14% on benchmark average.

Clarity on calibration propagation: It is ambiguous in Algorithm 1 whether calibration activations X and original outputs Y are collected statically from the unpruned model upfront, or sequentially propagated layer-by-layer as each sub-layer is pruned and rotated.

strengths: Sound mathematical formulation: Casting post-pruning error compensation as an Orthogonal Procrustes problem is principled, yielding an exact closed-form solution via SVD that avoids ill-conditioned unconstrained linear updates.

Geometric regularization: By constraining the parameter update to an orthogonal transformation (and isotropic scaling), the method preserves feature angles, relative lengths, and norms, effectively preventing overfitting on small calibration datasets.

Comprehensive layer-level ablations: The analysis clarifies where rotation compensation is most impactful (e.g., updating o_proj vs. down_proj) and validates the failure of unconstrained least-squares updates.
weaknesses: Narrow experimental evaluation: Experiments are conducted exclusively on the original LLaMA-7B model from 2023. Modern benchmarks require validation across diverse architectures and larger/newer models (e.g., LLaMA-2/3, Mistral, or Qwen) to prove general applicability.

Marginal performance gains over baseline: Compared to FLAP, the improvements on downstream zero-shot accuracy in Table 2 are very small (e.g., +0.21% at 10% pruning, +0.25% at 20% pruning, and +0.14% at 30% pruning for Rot.+Scale, while Rot.-only is actually worse than FLAP at 30%). In many individual tasks (such as ARC-c and OBQA), FLAP outperforms RCPU.

Missing key structured pruning baselines: While SliceGPT (Ashkboos et al., 2024) is discussed in the related work, it is neither quantitatively compared against nor ablated, despite being one of the most prominent rotation-based structured compression methods for LLMs.

Conflation of contributions: The paper introduces both a new variance-aware pruning score and a rotation-based update. In the main comparison (Table 1 and Table 2), it is unclear whether FLAP was evaluated using the proposed variance score or its original score, making it hard to decouple how much gain comes from the score versus the rotation compensation.

Lack of wall-clock inference speedup: Structured pruning is primarily motivated by practical hardware acceleration. Table 4 reports pruning time and parameter reduction, but actual inference latency / throughput measurements (tokens/s) on target hardware are missing.

strengths: Clear motivation: The paper identifies a well-founded issue in post-pruning compensation, namely that unconstrained least-squares updates overfit under small calibration sets, causing severe geometric distortion.

Mathematically principled formulation: Formulating output realignment as an Orthogonal Procrustes problem provides an analytical, closed-form solution via SVD that strictly preserves inner products and norms.
Clarity and presentation: The manuscript is well-structured, easy to follow, and includes informative ablations on layer-specific updates (o_proj vs. down_proj) and calibration fitting.
weaknesses: Limited and outdated experimental evaluation: Experiments are conducted exclusively on LLaMA-7B (an older first-generation model). There are no evaluations on modern open-source architectures (e.g., LLaMA-2/3, Mistral, Qwen) or across different parameter scales (e.g., 13B, 70B).

Marginal empirical gains: Across the zero-shot reasoning benchmarks (Table 2), RCPU achieves only marginal improvements over the FLAP baseline (e.g., mean accuracy gains of +0.21% at 10% pruning, +0.25% at 20%, and +0.14% at 30%). Given typical benchmark variance and the absence of error bars across multiple calibration seeds, these gains are barely discernible from noise.

Missing relevant baselines: Key post-training structured pruning methods such as SliceGPT are discussed in related work but omitted from the empirical comparisons. Comparing against contemporary structured compression techniques is essential.

Heuristic nature and dimensional inconsistency of the scoring metric: The variance-aware score multiplies the activation norm by the variance (Eq. 10), which creates an inconsistent dimensional scaling (norm is linear in activation scale, whereas variance is quadratic). There is little theoretical justification for why variance was selected over standard deviation, nor why this specific heuristic weighting is optimal.

Mild pruning ratios and lack of real-world speedup measurements: The experiments evaluate only modest pruning ratios up to 30%, omitting high-sparsity regimes (e.g., 40-50%) where structured pruning degradation is most severe. Furthermore, while pruning time is reported, the paper does not report actual wall-clock inference speedups or memory footprint measurements during inference on real deployment hardware.
